title: Product Decision Journal
project: AI Services POC — BambooHR Consultant App

outcomes.title: Make design work in Claude Code legible and transferable
outcomes.reasoning: Designer transitioned from Figma to Claude Code. Two things were lost: (1) the visual canvas showing all artboards/branches/iterations at a glance, and (2) the ability to hand off a project file where a new designer can see everything that's been designed and understand why. Without these, a Claude Code project is opaque to anyone who wasn't in the original sessions.

evidence.quote: If I take over a project that another designer has worked on, I just want to talk to Claude and get answers on any questions I have: why things were done a certain way, what the decisions were at critical junctures.
A coworker was using a spreadsheet to keep track of ideas, experiments done, results found. My reaction was: I want to be able to ask Claude about this instead of looking through a spreadsheet.

outcomes.title: BHR consultants can work as fast as they think
outcomes.reasoning: The AI Services POC is building tools for BambooHR HR consultants who manage multiple clients. The core product question: can we make the consultant's daily workflow — switching contexts, managing payroll, onboarding, benefits — feel effortless? The app should disappear and let the consultant focus on their clients, not the tool.

opportunities.title: Consultants need a fast, intuitive way to switch between client workspaces
opportunities.reasoning: HR consultants manage 5-50 clients and switch between them frequently throughout the day. The core UX question: how does a consultant select which client they're working with? Must feel fast, professional, and not lose context when switching. Prototyped 6 approaches (A-F), narrowed to 3 active candidates (B, C, E).

opportunities.title: HRCs lose sight of plan progress when it scrolls out of chat
opportunities.reasoning: The #1 visibility gap: ActionCard renders inline in chat and scrolls away as conversation continues. HRCs can't monitor what the agent is doing without scrolling away from the conversation. Need plan progress AND chat visible simultaneously. Requirements: tiered visibility (milestones in chat, thinking expandable), auto+toggle behavior, pause/stop/edit controls, non-undoable action gates, plan history as archive, cross-client persistence.

evidence.quote: I can only look at it while it's running which is like 5 seconds.

opportunities.title: Designers can't see the landscape of what's been explored
opportunities.reasoning: In Figma, you copy an artboard and start changing it — the canvas shows the whole train of thought, the branches, dead ends. In Claude Code, there's no equivalent. You can't see what screens exist, what was tried, what was abandoned. The mental model lives only in the designer's head and the conversation history.

opportunities.title: No institutional memory — new designer can't understand why things are the way they are
opportunities.reasoning: When a designer takes over a project, step one is knowing what exists (inventory). Step two is understanding why decisions were made (narrative). The previous designer might not be around to explain. Today there's no artifact that captures this — you'd have to read through every conversation transcript.

solutions.title: Plan Panel — Approach A: Right Rail (side panel)
solutions.reasoning: Resizable panel to the right of chat (420px default), modeled on ArtifactPanel. Has a collapsed floating pill with progress ring when minimized. Rejected because it's visually identical to Approach C (split view) — both are right-side panels. No meaningful UX difference from the user's perspective. Architectural difference (page-level vs ChatView-internal) doesn't matter to the HRC.

solutions.title: Plan Panel — Approach B: Sticky Dock (top bar)
solutions.reasoning: Collapsible bar pinned above chat messages. Collapsed: 60px with status dot, title, progress bar, controls. Expanded: ~200px with step list and agent log. Zero horizontal space cost. Genuinely different UX from the side panel approaches. Parked because: interesting pattern that could work on client home pages for cross-client plan visibility, but for the chat view the split panel (C) gives more room for detail. May come back for dashboard/home use.

evidence.quote: B is interesting, and we might be able to use that on the client home page actually when a plan is running.

solutions.title: Plan Panel — Approach C: Split View (internal to ChatView)
solutions.reasoning: ChatView splits into two resizable panes — chat left, plan right (380px default). Internal to ChatView so page layout sees no change. Natural transition: when no plan is active, it's a single pane. Chosen because it provides the most detail space alongside chat, feels like a natural extension of the conversation, and the resize handle gives the HRC control.

solutions.title: Design Iteration Tracker (Tool 1)
solutions.reasoning: A visual tool for tracking the branching tree of ideas during active design work. Shows what's active, parked, rejected, and how ideas spawned from each other. This is the 'Figma canvas replacement' — externalizing the mental model of exploration. Addresses OP1 directly.

evidence.quote: It's just hard to keep the whole tree in your head of good ideas vs ideas to come back to later vs rejected ideas.

solutions.title: Product Decision Journal (Tool 2)
solutions.reasoning: A living record of the entire product discovery process — outcomes, opportunities, solutions, experiments, decisions. Claude maintains it automatically. Primary interface is conversational (ask Claude 'why did we choose X?'). Secondary interface is visual (OST graph). This is the handoff artifact — makes a project legible to newcomers. Addresses OP2 directly.

evidence.quote: The mental model I have here is automated AI meeting notes, where AI has listened to the meeting and captured todos, action items, etc.

solutions.title: Approach A: Card Grid — full-page client cards with click-to-enter
solutions.reasoning: Full-page grid of client cards. Click a card to enter that client's workspace. Good first impression and onboarding feel, but mode-switch friction persists — you leave the workspace to see the grid. Parked because the cards metaphor has potential on the main dashboard page or combined with another approach, but not as the primary client selector.

evidence.quote: The clients as cards view is interesting, but I don't know if this is the right place for it. I could see it coming back on the main dashboard page, or maybe we like this + another idea.

solutions.title: Approach B: Dropdown Switcher — compact dropdown in tab bar
solutions.reasoning: Compact dropdown trigger in the tab bar area. Open to search/switch clients. Attention indicator on trigger shows pending items. Minimal space usage, fast switching, ⌘K hint for power users. One of two front-runner approaches.

solutions.title: Approach C: Sidebar List — persistent collapsible client panel
solutions.reasoning: Persistent sidebar (w-56, collapsible to w-12) with client avatars, names, unread badges, urgency indicators, and search. Fastest switching — client is always one click away. Collapsible to reclaim space. The other front-runner approach.

solutions.title: Approach D: Breadcrumb Navigation — hierarchical nav with admin table
solutions.reasoning: Breadcrumb trail (All Clients > Client Name) with a filterable/sortable admin table for client selection. Good triage tool but killed because there's only one layer of breadcrumbs, so the pattern doesn't justify itself.

evidence.quote: Kill. It's only one layer of breadcrumbs.

solutions.title: Approach E: Tab Groups — multi-client grouped tabs in a single bar
solutions.reasoning: All clients' chat tabs visible in one bar, grouped by client with colored headers. Each group has a client avatar chip followed by that client's chat tabs. Interesting Chrome-like model. Not a front-runner but kept open out of curiosity to see if it can be made to work at scale.

evidence.quote: This one has promise, maybe just because of a perverse curiosity I have to see if it could be made to work. It's not a front runner but we could come back to it.

solutions.title: Approach F: Client Tabs Row — horizontal avatar row above tab bar
solutions.reasoning: Row of client avatar circles above the chat tab bar. Click avatar to switch client context. Killed because it's essentially a two-layer tab (avatar row + chat tab bar) and the designer doubts HRCs will embrace circles as client identity.

evidence.quote: Kill. It's basically like a two-layer tab. I don't think HRCs are going to be keen on the circles to represent clients.

solutions.title: Key decision: Two separate tools, not one
solutions.reasoning: Tool 1 (iteration tracker) is the workbench — used during active design. Tool 2 (decision journal) is the archive — used for handoff and institutional memory. Tool 1 feeds into Tool 2: exploration captured in the iteration tracker gets distilled into the decision journal as entries. They must stay separate because they serve different audiences and timescales. The iteration tracker can be referenced from a decision journal node but they have independent schemas and lifecycles.

experiments.title: Spreadsheet for tracking decisions
experiments.reasoning: A coworker's approach — tracking ideas, experiments, results in a spreadsheet. Rejected because: not queryable conversationally by Claude, not visual/spatial, flat structure can't represent an OST hierarchy, and the designer's reaction was 'I want to ask Claude about this, not look through a spreadsheet.'

experiments.title: Obsidian vault (folder of markdown files)
experiments.reasoning: One file per decision/opportunity/experiment, linked with [[wikilinks]]. Good for humans browsing, good for Claude to read/write. Rejected because: Obsidian's graph view is famously useless for comprehension (hairball), requires Obsidian as a dependency, and adds friction to adoption.

experiments.title: Single structured JSON + standalone HTML viewer
experiments.reasoning: Chosen for v1. Claude reads/writes JSON natively. Zero external dependencies — render it however you want with a standalone HTML file (proven pattern from the iteration tracker). JSON isn't fun to read raw, so it lives or dies by the viewer and Claude's ability to answer questions from it. Simplest path to a working v1.

experiments.title: Single markdown file with conventions (DECISIONS.md)
experiments.reasoning: Headings = outcomes, subheadings = opportunities, bullets = solutions. Claude can read/write trivially, humans can read in any editor. Rejected because: too unstructured for reliable querying, no graph view possible without a parser, and markdown conventions drift over time.

experiments.title: Notion as collaboration layer
experiments.reasoning: Notion databases can represent the OST relationally (Outcomes, Opportunities, Solutions, Experiments as linked databases). Multiple views of same data (kanban, table, gallery, timeline). Real-time collaboration built in. Official Notion MCP exists with full read/write (22 tools, create entries, update properties, write page content). Free plan works for solo + 10 guests. Deferred because: collaboration isn't a v1 requirement, and the local JSON approach proves the concept faster. But this is the path forward for scaling across the org.

evidence.quote: Official Notion MCP server, maintained by Notion. Setup is one command + OAuth. Claude can create databases, create entries, update properties, write page content. Cannot upload files or do bulk operations.
Unlimited pages and blocks for solo use. Databases and API fully available. Up to 10 guest collaborators. Pain points: 5MB file cap, 7-day version history, 1000 block limit for team workspaces.

experiments.title: Hybrid: local JSON + Notion sync
experiments.reasoning: Claude maintains a local JSON copy for querying and reasoning. Periodically syncs to/from Notion for collaboration. Trio maintains their FigJam OST, Claude reads it via MCP, reconciles with local copy. Described as 'janky but interesting' — doesn't require the trio to change behavior. Deferred to post-v1.

experiments.title: SQLite database
experiments.reasoning: Structured and queryable, Claude can read/write via bash. Powerful for complex queries. Rejected because: invisible without a viewer, overkill for most projects, adds complexity without proportional benefit over JSON for this use case.

experiments.title: Git-native approach (commit history + PR descriptions)
experiments.reasoning: No new artifact — decisions live in commit messages, PR descriptions, branch names. Claude synthesizes on demand. Rejected because: most commit messages are garbage, only works retroactively, and doesn't capture the reasoning/context that lives in conversation.

decisions.title: Prune client navigation prototypes: keep B, C, E — park A, kill D and F
decisions.reasoning: After building and reviewing all 6 client-selection approaches at v3 with full-width tab bars, the designer pruned the set. B (Dropdown) and C (Sidebar) are the strongest candidates — both switch-first approaches that feel fast for daily workflow. E (Tab Groups) stays open as an intriguing experiment. A (Card Grid) is parked — the cards-as-clients metaphor has potential but may belong on the dashboard, not here. D (Breadcrumb) is killed — only one layer of breadcrumbs, so the pattern doesn't add value. F (Client Tabs Row) is killed — essentially a two-layer tab with avatar circles; HRCs unlikely to embrace circles for client identity.

evidence.quote: A: park. The clients as cards view is interesting, but I don't know if this is the right place for it. I could see it coming back on the main dashboard page.
D: kill. It's only one layer of breadcrumbs.
E: this one has promise, maybe just because of a perverse curiosity I have to see if it could be made to work.
F: kill. It's basically like a two-layer tab. I don't think HRCs are going to be keen on the circles to represent clients.

decisions.title: Plan panel: kill A, park B for home page, ship C (split view)
decisions.reasoning: Built 3 plan panel approaches (A: right rail, B: sticky dock, C: split view). A and C were visually identical — both right-side panels, just different render locations. Killed A. B (dock) is genuinely different UX (horizontal bar, zero horizontal cost) but limited detail space. Parked B with the insight that it could work on client home pages for cross-client plan visibility. Chose C (split view) for chat because it gives the most detail space and feels like a natural extension of the conversation.

evidence.quote: Get rid of A. B is interesting, and we might be able to use that on the client home page actually when a plan is running. So park it for now and we'll continue with C.

decisions.title: Claude auto-maintains the journal via implicit capture
decisions.reasoning: The 'AI meeting notes' model: Claude watches for decision moments in conversation and logs them automatically. The designer doesn't change their behavior. Explicit capture ('/decision' command) also available as a supplement. Hook-based capture (post-session review) is interesting for later. The key insight: the tool fails if it requires manual curation — it needs to be passive like meeting notes AI.
openItems: Exact trigger heuristics for implicit capture not yet defined
Post-session hook design not yet specified

decisions.title: Notion is the collaboration path, but not v1
decisions.reasoning: The scaling story: (1) Now: local JSON, solo + conversation with Claude. (2) Soon: show the workflow works, org buys Notion, sync local journal to Notion. (3) Later: standardized template, every project gets an OST workspace. Collaboration is not a v1 requirement, but the architecture should point toward it. The designer is pioneering a process to scale across the org.

evidence.quote: Collaboration is not a hard requirement for v1, but I'm pioneering a process here that I would really like to be able to scale across the org.

decisions.title: The ideal end-state is FigJam OST with Claude read/write
decisions.reasoning: If Claude could write to FigJam, the solution would be obvious: trio maintains OST in FigJam (as they should already be doing), Claude reads and writes via MCP, humans see it natively, no duplicate work. Currently blocked by FigJam MCP being read-only. This is the north star — every intermediate solution is a stepping stone to this.

openQuestions.title: Can the plan dock (Approach B) work on the client home page?
openQuestions.context: Designer noted the sticky dock pattern could show running plans on client home/overview screens, not just inside chat. Would give cross-client plan visibility without navigating into a chat. Worth exploring when we build the client home page.

openQuestions.title: What are the exact heuristics for implicit decision capture?
openQuestions.context: Claude needs to recognize decision moments in conversation: 'let's go with X', 'that doesn't work because...', 'oh interesting, what if...'. What patterns trigger a journal entry vs. are just normal conversation?

openQuestions.title: What should the OST graph viewer look like?
openQuestions.context: User wants a node-and-edge graph (not just a card list). Should show dead ends grayed out, active paths highlighted. Needs to be zoomable/pannable. Should also collapse to a flat rich-content list. Standalone HTML, zero dependencies.

openQuestions.title: When and how to introduce Notion sync?
openQuestions.context: After v1 proves the concept. Needs: Notion MCP write working reliably, a database schema that maps to this JSON schema, a sync strategy (one-way push? bidirectional merge? conflict resolution?).

openQuestions.title: How does the trio's existing OST practice (if any) integrate?
openQuestions.context: Trios should be building OSTs. If they already are (in FigJam, Miro, etc.), the journal shouldn't duplicate that work. Ideal: Claude reads the trio's OST and enriches it with design-session details.
